$comment: Single source of truth for the nightly performance run, read by both the k6
entrypoint (packages/api-workload/main.js) and every Node-side step.
Every scenario uses a constant-arrival-rate executor: offered load is fixed
rather than derived from how fast the system answers, which is what makes one
night's numbers comparable to the next.
Scenarios run one after another rather than together. Concurrent scenarios
would contend for the same database and each one's latency would then depend
on the others' workloads, which makes an SLO breach impossible to attribute.
THE OFFERED LOAD IS CAPPED BY THE API'S OWN RATE LIMIT, NOT BY CHOICE.
A workspace key is allowed `requestsPerMinuteBudget` requests per rolling
minute (100 today — see docs/methodology.md). The
limiter's window is per key and does not reset between scenarios, so the
constraint is on the whole run: no rolling minute anywhere in it may exceed
the budget. That is why the authenticated scenarios sit at 1 request/second
and earn their sample counts from duration instead of concurrency: ten
minutes at 1 request/second is 600 samples, so p95 rests on ~30 observations
and p99 on ~6 rather than the 6 and 1 that two minutes would give. It also
means these numbers measure latency under light load: they will catch an
added query, a lost index or a payload that grew, and will not catch lock
contention or a capacity cliff. `pnpm perf:run` reads the key's actual limit
and refuses to start rather than producing a run full of 429s.
`platform-baseline` is unauthenticated, so it spends no budget and can offer
real concurrency.
Changing `rate`, `timeUnit`, `duration`, `preAllocatedVUs` or the budget
changes what is being measured, so it invalidates the baseline: bump
`workloadVersion` when you do and the analyzer starts a fresh baseline
population rather than comparing across incomparable runs.
SLO TARGETS ARE BUDGETS ABOVE THE NETWORK FLOOR, NOT ABSOLUTE MILLISECONDS.
The runner sits some distance from the deployment, and that distance is not
the API's to answer for: the first nightly, from GitHub Actions, put an
empty build-info read at 187ms p50 (ten at a time) and the entitlement check
at 107ms p50, then reported seven authenticated scenarios as breaching
120–250ms absolute targets — the round trip alone was most of those budgets.
So `network-floor` (`floorScenario`) offers the same empty request at the
authenticated scenarios' own rate and concurrency, and each authenticated
scenario declares `sloP95AboveFloorMs`: the collector resolves its target for
the run as the floor's p50 plus that budget, and records both. A scenario is
then judged on the work the API did, wherever the run was measured from.
`platform-baseline` keeps an absolute `sloP95Ms`: it offers ten concurrent
requests and exists to catch cold-start and concurrency behaviour, which a
floor measured at one request per second would not see. The floor itself has
an absolute target too, because a slow floor is a platform finding.
The budgets are the draft targets from docs/methodology.md ("SLO hypotheses"),
less the floor they were implicitly carrying. They are hypotheses to confirm
against the first baselines, not settled contracts.
Write scenarios cost storage that outlives the run: the platform keeps usage
events as billing records, so archiving the probe customer in teardown does
not reclaim them. At the sizes below one run writes ~51k events (50k of them from
usage-ingest-batch), which is the figure to revisit if the target environment's retention becomes a concern.

scenarios.name: network-floor
scenarios.description: The same empty build-info read as platform-baseline, at the authenticated scenarios' own rate and concurrency. Its p50 is the floor every sloP95AboveFloorMs target is resolved from.

scenarios.name: platform-baseline
scenarios.description: Unauthenticated build-info read: network and cold-start floor, carrying no query cost. A move here explains moves everywhere else.

scenarios.name: entitlement-check
scenarios.description: Single feature check on the customer's hot path.

scenarios.name: entitlement-batch
scenarios.description: Multi-feature check in one round trip, the path an SDK takes on page load.

scenarios.name: customer-reads
scenarios.description: Paginated customer list across the full seeded population.

scenarios.name: catalog-reads
scenarios.description: Published products and plans, the pricing-page path.

scenarios.name: usage-ingest
scenarios.description: Single metered event stamped at ingest time, the write-side hot path.

scenarios.name: usage-ingest-backdated
scenarios.description: Single metered event carrying its own `occurredAt`, the disruption-catch-up path. Split from the real-time case so ingestion-lag metrics stay interpretable.

scenarios.name: usage-ingest-batch
scenarios.description: Bulk ingest at the documented 500-item ceiling. Paced at one request per six seconds: each iteration writes 500 billing rows that outlive the run.
